tools.name: The Twelve-Prompt Voice Capture Brand Brief
tools.content:
# The Voice Capture Brand Brief
**Your single-source brand voice document. Fill in every field in your own words — rough, direct, and specific. This is not for anyone else to read; it is the source your copy pulls from.**

---

## SECTION 1 — YOUR WORDS, NOT THE CATEGORY

**Prompt 1 — The phrase you say on every discovery call**
> What's the sentence you find yourself repeating to almost every prospect — the one that feels so obvious to you that you almost didn't bother saying it, but the client always writes it down?

[Write it verbatim, in the words you actually use on the call — not the polished version]

---

**Prompt 2 — The word you'd never use**
> Every coach has a category word they find hollow. "Transformation." "Aligned." "Empowered." Name three words your clients use in their intake forms or discovery calls that feel accurate but that you would never put in your own copy — and write the word you use instead.

| Their word | Your word instead |
|---|---|
| [e.g. "stuck"] | [e.g. "the Sunday-evening weight"] |
| [CLIENT WORD 2] | [YOUR WORD 2] |
| [CLIENT WORD 3] | [YOUR WORD 3] |

---

**Prompt 3 — The explanation you give that nobody else gives**
> What's the one thing about your methodology or approach that you explain differently from every other coach in your space — the angle that makes a prospect say "I've never heard it put that way"?

[Write the explanation as you'd give it to a skeptical friend — no jargon, no capitals on every word]

---

## SECTION 2 — THE TUESDAY-MORNING MOMENT

**Prompt 4 — The exact scene, not the category of pain**
> Your ideal client doesn't feel "overwhelmed." They feel something specific — at a specific moment, on a specific kind of morning. Describe the moment they hit rock bottom in physical, environmental detail: where are they sitting, what are they looking at, what have they just done or just avoided doing?

[Write the scene. Name the object they're staring at. Name the tab they've had open for two weeks. Name the thing they told themselves they'd do after the school run.]

---

**Prompt 5 — The internal monologue at that moment**
> What does your ideal client say to themselves in that scene — the exact words, including the ones they'd be embarrassed to admit?

[Write the internal monologue in first person, as they'd say it. "I've been saying I'm going to write this page for three weeks and I've opened a new Google doc four times and closed it."]

---

**Prompt 6 — What they do instead of solving it**
> Name the specific avoidance behaviour they reach for when the blank page wins. (Not "they get distracted" — the specific thing: they reorganise Notion, they go back through someone else's sales page for "research," they book another discovery call to buy time.)

[Name the specific avoidance behaviour, as concretely as you can]

---

## SECTION 3 — YOUR VOICE IN THE WILD

**Prompt 7 — A sentence from a client message you've saved**
> Find a real message — a WhatsApp, a Slack message, an email — where a client described the result of working with you in their own words. Copy it here verbatim, typos and all.

[Paste the raw client message — do not tidy it up]

---

**Prompt 8 — A sentence you wrote that you're proud of**
> Find something you wrote — a caption, an email line, a voice note you transcribed — where you read it back and thought "yes, that's actually me." Copy that sentence here.

[Paste the sentence — then write one line on what made it feel right]

What made it feel right: [write it plain]

---

**Prompt 9 — The analogy you keep reaching for**
> When you explain what coaching with you is like, what's the comparison, metaphor, or analogy you find yourself coming back to? (Not the one you think sounds good — the one that actually falls out of your mouth.)

[Write the analogy, and the context in which you usually reach for it]

---

## SECTION 4 — THE EDGES OF YOUR VOICE

tools.name: The Voice-Check Filter: 5 Questions Before You Hit Send
tools.content:
# The Voice-Check Filter
**Run this against any piece of copy before it goes live. Pull up your completed Brand Brief alongside it.**

---

## Before you hit send / publish, answer these five questions:

**1. Does the opening line name the scene, or just the category?**
- ☐ It names a specific scene (a moment, an object, a behaviour) — **keep it**
- ☐ It names a category ("overwhelm", "frustration", "burnout") with nothing concrete attached — **rewrite the first sentence using Prompt 4 from your Brief**

---

**2. Does any sentence contain a word from your "never use" column?**
- ☐ No — clear
- ☐ Yes — replace with your "use instead" word from Prompt 2 of your Brief

*Quick check: scan for "transformation", "aligned", "journey", "empower", "pivot", "authentic" — and any other word you logged in your Brief. If it's in there and you don't own it, cut it.*

---

**3. Is there one sentence in this piece you couldn't have borrowed from another coach's page?**
- ☐ Yes — underline it. That sentence is load-bearing. Make sure it's early.
- ☐ No — find your Prompt 9 analogy and build it into the piece before publishing.

---

**4. Does this copy make the reader feel the thing you named in Prompt 10 — even accidentally?**
- ☐ No — clear
- ☐ Yes — identify the sentence that creates that tone and rewrite it using your Prompt 8 proof-of-voice sentence as a register guide

---

**5. If your most self-aware client read this cold, would they think "she gets it" or "this sounds like everyone else"?**
- ☐ "She gets it" — publish
- ☐ "Everyone else" — go back to Prompt 5 (the internal monologue) and add one line that quotes the thought your client hasn't admitted out loud

---

**If you checked all five and cleared them: hit send.**

If you rewrote based on this checklist and the piece still feels off — the problem is usually that you're writing to the category of pain (Prompt 4 wasn't specific enough). Go back and add one physical detail to the opening scene.

tools.name: The Discovery Call Voice Mining SOP
tools.content:
# The Discovery Call Voice Mining SOP
**Run this process after any discovery call or coaching session where a client said something that stopped you. Four steps, done while the conversation is still fresh.**

---

## STEP 1 — FLAG THE MOMENT (do this immediately after the call ends)

Before you close the Zoom window or check your phone, write down — in a notes app, a voice memo, anywhere — the answer to this one question:

> *"What was the one sentence my client said today that I could have written into a sales page?"*

Write it verbatim. Do not paraphrase. Include the hedge words, the filler, the trailing-off. "It's like… I know what I should be doing, I just keep finding reasons not to open the document."

This is the raw material. The paraphrase is yours. The verbatim quote is theirs — and theirs is what converts.

---

## STEP 2 — SORT INTO YOUR BRIEF (takes 3–5 minutes)

Open your Voice Capture Brand Brief. Look at what you just captured and ask:

| Question | If yes, drop it here |
|---|---|
| Is this the Tuesday-morning scene in their words? | Prompt 4 or 5 — add it as a real example |
| Is this a word or phrase I'd never use myself? | Prompt 2 — add to the "avoid" column |
| Is this the internal monologue — the thing they'd be embarrassed to admit? | Prompt 5 — add verbatim |
| Is this a way they described their result that surprised me? | Prompt 7 — add as a second proof quote |
| Is this an analogy I didn't expect but recognised immediately? | Prompt 9 — note it as a field-sourced comparison |

If it doesn't fit a prompt, paste it at the bottom of the Brief under **"Raw Voice Bank"** — it belongs somewhere even if you don't know where yet.

---

## STEP 3 — UPDATE YOUR VOICE SNAPSHOT

Check whether anything you just added changes your top-of-doc Voice Snapshot (the six-line summary at the end of the Brief).

Specifically:
- Did the client give you a sharper version of the Tuesday-morning scene? Update Prompt 4 to match.
- Did they use a phrase in Prompt 5 that's better than what you had? Replace it.
- Did they describe your result in a way that's more specific than your current Prompt 7 quote? Swap it in.

The Brief is a living document. The version that converts is the one that's most current, not the one you filled in first.

---

## STEP 4 — APPLY IT TO THE NEXT PIECE OF COPY YOU WRITE

The next time you open a blank page — email, caption, sales page section — start by reading your Voice Snapshot (the six-line block at the top of your Brief) before you type a single word.

Then write the opening line of your piece by completing this sentence:

> *"My reader is [location from Prompt 4], staring at [specific object or tab or task], telling themselves [verbatim internal monologue from Prompt 5]..."*

You don't have to publish that sentence. You just have to write it first, so your copy lands in the right moment before it lands on the right page.

---

**What this SOP gives you:** A Brief that gets sharper every time you run a call, rather than a static document you fill in once and ignore. The coaches whose copy accumulates coherence over time are the ones doing this step — not because they're better writers, but because they have more current raw material.
tools.instructions: A four-step process to run after any discovery call or client session to pull raw voice material directly into your Brand Brief — keeps your document alive and current.

tools.name: The 'Blank Page to First Line' Sentence Starter Bank
tools.content:
# The Blank Page to First Line Sentence Starter Bank
**Each starter below connects directly to a prompt in your Brand Brief. Find the one that fits the piece you're writing, fill in the brackets using your Brief answers, and you have a first line that's already in your voice.**

---

## FOR EMAIL SUBJECT LINES
*(Pull the specific object or behaviour from Prompt 4 or 6)*

1. `The [SPECIFIC OPEN TAB / DOCUMENT / TASK] you've had open since [DAY OF WEEK]`
2. `What I stopped saying on discovery calls (and started writing instead)`
3. `The thing you told yourself you'd do after [SPECIFIC SMALL TASK FROM PROMPT 6]`
4. `Why your [sales page / launch email / caption] sounds like everyone else's (it's not the writing)`

---

## FOR EMAIL OPENING LINES
*(Connects to Prompt 4 — the scene — and Prompt 5 — the internal monologue)*

5. `If you've opened a new Google doc this week, written [FIRST LINE YOUR IDEAL CLIENT WRITES], and closed it again — this email is about that specific moment.`

6. `There's a particular kind of [DAY OF WEEK] morning that my clients describe almost identically: [SCENE FROM PROMPT 4 IN ONE SENTENCE]. This is what I've learned about it.`

7. `[CLIENT VERBATIM QUOTE FROM PROMPT 5] — that's a real sentence from a real discovery call. If you've said a version of that to yourself, keep reading.`

---

## FOR SALES PAGE OPENING PARAGRAPHS
*(Connects to Prompts 4, 5, and your Prompt 11 contrarian position)*

8. `You don't have a writing problem. You have a [YOUR PHRASE FROM PROMPT 1] problem — and those two things require completely different solutions.`

9. `The [SPECIFIC AVOIDANCE BEHAVIOUR FROM PROMPT 6] isn't procrastination. It's what happens when you sit down to write from a voice you haven't formally captured yet. [YOUR ONE-SENTENCE POSITIONING STATEMENT FROM PROMPT 12].`

10. `Every [COACHING NICHE] I've worked with can tell me exactly what their client needs. Almost none of them can tell me the [SPECIFIC SCENE FROM PROMPT 4] — the moment just before the client decides they need help. That gap is where the conversion lives.`

---

## FOR CAPTIONS
*(Short, scene-first — Prompt 4 in one line, then the turn)*

11. `[OBJECT FROM PROMPT 4]. [AVOIDANCE BEHAVIOUR FROM PROMPT 6]. [YOUR CONTRARIAN POSITION FROM PROMPT 11 IN ONE SENTENCE].`

12. `The [CLIENT WORD FROM PROMPT 2 "AVOID" COLUMN] everyone keeps using isn't wrong — it's just not specific enough to help. Here's what I say instead: [YOUR WORD FROM PROMPT 2 "USE" COLUMN], which means [PLAIN LANGUAGE EXPLANATION].`

---

**How to use this bank:**
Don't pick the starter that sounds best in the abstract. Pick the one that requires the most specific fill-in from your Brief — the more specific the fill-in, the harder it is for anyone else to have written the same line. That's where your voice lives.

promise: Fill in all twelve prompts and you own a living brand voice document — one single page that every email, sales page, and caption you write pulls from so your copy accumulates coherence instead of re-inventing itself with each launch.
howToUse: This is your Voice Capture Brand Brief Template — a fill-in document that extracts your real brand voice across twelve targeted prompts and assembles the answers into a single-page reference document every piece of copy you write from here forward inherits. Open it alongside a recording of a recent discovery call or a screenshot of a client message, work through each prompt in raw, unpolished language, and when you're done you'll have a permanent source document that ends the "start from zero" writing problem. Keep it open in a browser tab every time you sit down to write.

nextStep.body: Your Voice Capture Brand Brief is your foundation for every copy exercise in the programme from here forward. The next time a module asks you to write a sales page section, a launch email, or a discovery-call invitation, open your completed Brief alongside the module — specifically your Voice Snapshot and your Prompt 5 internal monologue — before you write a single word. This is how the programme's Client Psychology Reverse-Map method lands in your actual voice rather than someone else's: the Reverse-Map tells you which moment to write to; your Brief gives you the exact words to write it in. They work together.
